Abstract: The paper discusses the possibility of engaging gig workers via an algorithm-driven management system that relies on ma-chine learning with the help of a predictive analytics framework. Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems
Abstract: Mechanistic algorithmic management is widely implemented in online labor platforms (OLPs) to ensure consistent delivery of high-quality services by their workers. To address humanized needs that are overlooked by algorithms, workers may use cheating tools to discover and exploit algorithmic loopholes. This poses challenges to the efficient operation of OLPs and markets. With the goal of facilitating OLPs to foster humanistic algorithmic management and reduce workers’ cheating behavior, this study constructs a two-player evolutionary game model, which is applied to characterize the dynamic decision-making processes of both players regarding algorithmic management. From a theoretical perspective, this study identifies four equilibrium strategies at different game stages and deduces the stability and constraints of these strategies, with “humanistic algorithmic management” and “no cheating” serving as the ideal strategies. Further, the data from Guangzhou’s Didi and Suzhou’s Amap platform and numerical simulation methods are adopted to analyze the impact of key factors on OLPs and workers’ decision-making at different game stages. These factors include government regulation, platform regulation, cheating efficiency, negative utility, and social learning, not just costs and benefits. Finally, this study elucidates the co-constitutive relationship between platform algorithms and workers’ behavior, confirms workers’ agency in the establishment of humanistic algorithmic management systems, and provides practical insights into how platforms can improve the performance and well-being of their employees.

Document Title: Re-Thinking Algorithmic Control: Common Assumptions, Controversies, Misconceptions
Publication Title: 2025 Eleventh International Conference on eDemocracy & eGovernment (ICEDEG)
Abstract: Algorithmic control, that is the use of algorithms to govern individual, organizational, and societal behaviors, has become a central topic in both academic and public discourse. Despite its widespread impact, the concept remains ambiguously defined, with significant variation in interpretations. This paper critically examines several common assumptions about algorithmic control, which have shaped its understanding in the literature. These include the belief that algorithmic control primarily serves to align capital and labor, operates independently of human intervention, is inherently rational and formalized, is a novel phenomenon, and is more opaque than human oversight. By unpacking these assumptions, the paper argues that algorithmic control transcends simplistic narratives, revealing its complex and multifaceted nature. It highlights the limitations of current frameworks of thinking, particularly those focused narrowly on labor platforms, and calls for a broader conceptualization that acknowledges the diverse purposes and dynamics of algorithmic control across different contexts.

Abstract: With the spread of digital technologies and mobile applications, a new way of working has emerged - the so-called “gig economy”. In it, people work through online platforms (such as Uber, Glovo, etc.), performing short tasks for pay. They are not employees in the traditional sense, but rather selfemployed individuals who are bound by the rules of the platforms. These platforms use algorithms that automatically distribute tasks, monitor the performance of workers and even decide who to remove from work. This type of management, called “algorithmic management”, is based entirely on modern information and communication infrastructure - cloud services, GPS, mobile applications and large data sets (Big Data). The study examines both the benefits (such as speed, efficiency and automation) and the serious ethical and legal challenges of this model. Topics such as lack of transparency in algorithmic decisions, violated labor rights, digital surveillance and the inability to protect against unlawful actions by the system come to the fore. The research emphasizes the need to balance technological efficiency with the protection of human rights. Good practices are proposed, such as including the human factor in important decisions and using transparent and open algorithms to avoid unethical treatment of gig economy workers.

Document Title: Human in the Loop: Understanding Employee Perception in AI-Based Performance Management System
Authors: M. Arslan; A. Ghezel; N. E. H. Tarabah; M. A. Selçuk; N. u. Saba
Author Affiliations: Ibn Haldun University, Istanbul, Turkey; Ibn Haldun University, Istanbul, Turkey; Ibn Haldun University, Istanbul, Turkey; Ibn Haldun University, Istanbul, Turkey; Ibn Haldun University, Istanbul, Turkey
Abstract: As organizations increasingly deploy algorithmic management systems to support performance evaluation, employee perceptions of AI-based performance management systems remain underexplored, particularly in knowledge-intensive environments where performance cannot be reduced to standardized metrics alone. This study examines how employees perceived and experienced an internally developed AI-based performance management system structured around the planning, monitoring, and review stages of the performance management cycle. Using a qualitative case study design, 19 semi-structured interviews were analyzed through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, supported by MAXQDA. Four themes were identified: emotionally-disconnected efficiency, task-bound trust, human-in-the-loop safeguard, and algorithmic fairness tension. Employees valued AI for speed, objectivity, documentation, and reduced managerial favoritism, but raised concerns about impersonal feedback, surveillance-like monitoring, contextual blindness, hidden bias, and opacity. Extending prior task-dependent algorithm-trust research, the findings show that AI-PMS legitimacy is not shaped by task type alone, but by the combined configuration of task type, performance-management stage, system transparency, and human oversight. AI was perceived as more legitimate for quantifiable KPI based evaluation, but less legitimate for qualitative, relational, developmental, and career consequential judgments. The study contributes to algorithmic management and AI-HRM research by moving beyond binary acceptance or resistance models toward a conditional legitimacy framework. For managers responsible for developing and implementing AI-based performance management systems, the findings highlight the importance of task-calibrated AI deployment, human-in-the-loop governance, transparent evaluation logic, and empathetic feedback practices to support the effective use of AI in critical HR functions such as performance management.
Author Keywords: AI-based performance management system;algorithmic management;human-in-the-loop;task-contingent legitimacy;employee perceptions;human-AI collaboration
